title: Duchy of Aquitaine
capsule: The Duchy of Aquitaine was one of the largest territorial principalities of medieval France, spanning the southwest between the Loire and the Pyrenees and including Gascony, with major centres at Poitiers and Bordeaux. Under Duke William IX (r. 1086–1126), reputed the first troubadour, the ducal court became a fountainhead of Occitan lyric, and his granddaughter Eleanor of Aquitaine carried the duchy through her marriages to Louis VII of France (1137) and then Henry II of England (1152), binding it to the Plantagenet realm. For the remainder of the period the duchy—reduced largely to Gascony around Bordeaux under the terms of Anglo-French settlements such as the Treaty of Paris (1259)—was a chronically contested borderland whose suzerainty pitted the kings of England, as dukes, against the French crown through the opening campaigns of the Hundred Years' War.
attestation: Boundaries from Seshat Cliopatria (Bennett et al., Scientific Data 2025; CC BY 4.0), digitized from standard historical atlases at ~0.07° resolution. The duchy's boundaries shifted substantially across different political phases; English Gascony's borders are documented through treaty records and administrative rolls, while earlier Carolingian and early Capetian extent is less precisely mapped.
